doc.title: Peter Appleyard interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, October 4, 2012

title: Calvin Jackson accepted in Toronto, and Oscar Peterson's haircut
summary: Calvin Jackson was accepted on his talent in Canada, while Oscar Peterson was once refused a haircut.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: No. But in Toronto, or where you lived, when the black musicians came up there was it, did they have issues?

This man Calvin Jackson was Afro-American, and was immediately accepted for his talent. He was an incredible arranger. He did lovely music on the “American in Paris” I think, and some of these major MGM productions, with Johnny Green, and an incredible soloist. He studied at Juilliard with degrees and what-have-you, and consequently he had incredible technique, classical and jazz. He was more of a classically-orientated player, but still could play. The changes that he used to play were just so gorgeous. Yeah, and he was accepted. He had his own radio show. He was doing a television show weekly, one week with a big band then with a small group, and he had all the guests there. He had Ella there, and all kinds of people. Then he used to arrange for three or four of the major television shows. And so there was no prejudice there. There weren’t that many black players in Canada, not in that time. Archie Alleyne was one prominent one who was a very good drummer. He’s still around. Bill Britto travelled, and Wray Downes is teaching at Concordia University. He played a lot like Oscar. And with Oscar of course, he suffered with the prejudice thing. He told me once he went to get his haircut in Hamilton and the guy wouldn’t cut his hair.
